description: Placeholder Kanji

We start our journey of over 2000 kanji with a single stroke. The kanji for one is but a single horizontal line written from left to right. Any learner of Japanese will likely have encountered this kanji as one of, if not the first kanji they learn, and it is easy to see why.

The character for two is, unsurprisingly, made up of two lines. The top line, which is written first, is also slightly shorter than the below line. Though Japanese still use kanji to represent numbers, depending on the context, Arabic numerals are also commonly used, so don't be surprised if you see a '2' appear when perusing a Japanese text.
The character for three is made up of a three horizontal lines. Once again, pay close attention to the size of each line when writing out this kanji.

If you were expecting a kanji with four lines to continue the pattern, then you will be disappointed by this kanji. In general, a kanji won't be introduced without first introudcing the elements that comprise it, but an exception has been made for the kanji relating to numbers. The character shows two 'human legs' which have been 'pent in' by a box-shaped enclosure.

This somewhat unique collection of strokes represents the number five. If you cover up the left had side of this kanji, you can sort of make out the Arabic numeral 5. This one may be a bit of a stretch but this should help you keep this kanji apart from the other numbers.

The kanji for six is actually made up of two elements 'pot lid' and 'animal legs', both of which we will learn in the next few chapters. For now, just remember the four strokes that make up this kanji.
This character for seven has the visual appearance of a so-called 'French seven' that has been flipped upside down.
This character, representing eight, also consists of two strokes, though this time they do not intersect.
Keep the stroke order in mind when learning this kanji to help keep it distinct from the similar looking kanji 力.
Another two stroke kanji, only this time the strokes form a very simple plus shape.
A simple pictogram of an open mouth. The stroke order is exactly the same as with 四 except for th dangling 'human legs'.
To keep this kanji distinct from 口, a single line was added before the final bottom stroke.
vocabulary: 一日・いちにち・ついたち

description: The first stroke for this kanji curves to the left in much the same way as the first stroke of 九 does. This kanji is a pictogram of a moon.
The kanji for evening also represents a moon. Here the moon is somewhat distorted when compared to 月, almost as though the evening has not yet fully surrended to the night.
This kanji represents a rice field that has been split into four. Pay close attention to the stroke order whne writing this kanji.

This kanji is a pictogram of a tree. The first stroke represents the leafy boughs of the tree, with the second stroke representing its trunk. Finally the two downward sweeping strokes represent the trees roots anchoring it down.
The three vertical parts of this kanji represent three mountain peaks with the central peak being taller than the other two.
Keep this character distinct from 右, by making sure the second stroke does not cross above the first. Here the small 'mouth' is representative of a little 'stone'.
The kanji for eye looks similar to 日 but with two inner strokes instead of one. Imagine the two inner strokes representing two eyelids with an invisible pupil interposed between them.

The kanji for shellfish itself consists of the element for 'eye' and the 'animal legs' we encountered in 六. The kanji represents a pictogram of the shell of a shellfish with two small legs to help it walk on the sea floor.
Whether this kanji represents a bent arm or a plow is still debated, but this kanji is used for the idea of 'power'.

Here we see a 'mouth' with sound waves coming out as represented by the first four strokes. Note that in print, the first stroke appears as a vertical stroke, but when written by hand the stroke is written as downward 'drop'. From time to time, we will see that the print form of a kanji doesn't always match up with how it would be written by hand.
Combining the characters for the sun 日 and moon 月 creates a kanji meaning 'bright'. It's easy to relate this kanji to the two brightest things seen within the sky, those being the sun and the moon.

The kanji for 'old' is made up of the elements 'ten' and 'mouth'. Instead of using these keywords, it may be best to think of the 'ten' as a 'cross'-shaped gravestone above an opening in the ground which presumably leads to an old crypt. Here we see why sometimes having more than one name or idea associated with an element can help create a more memorable mnemonic.
This kanji depicts a 'sun' rising over a 'cross' creating the picture of church bells ringing out in the early morning.
A 'male' is depicted here as someone flexing their arm in a rice field, providing the physical strength for the harvest.
A rock is simply a stone the size of a mountain. This kanji really needs no further explanation.
This kanji represents quite an abstract concept. Imagine a forrest containing trees with eyes which watch over each other. Each tree watches another tree to ensure their mutual safety.
A tree with a line striking through its trunk came to mean 'book'. Imagine a tree being chopped down near the roots, the wood later being used to create the paper for the books.

This kanji always reminds me of one of those complicated architectural blueprints with lots of annotating 'words', 'crosses' indicating the important parts of the plan, and of course the all important measurements.

'Say five mouths' clearly refers to the five senses used to fully communicate across a language barrier. Of course we must use our mouths to say words, but we must also use our other senses to fully appreciate the language and culture.

A 'mouth' above a 'shellfish' could represent someone eating lots of seafood, but here, the mouth is in fact eating all the 'money' generated by the company they work for, presumably to the dismay of the big bosses.
Imagine an evening so 'dark' that the only way to identify your friend in a crowd is if they open their 'mouth' and say their name.
Sometimes, the simple reduplication of an element can create a new kanji. Here we have 'evening' written twice to mean 'many', demonstrating the many evenings we have to rest.
'Mouth' is reduplicated here three times to create a kanji meaning 'goods'. When buying new goods, it's important to think of how many mouths you need to feed in order to purchase the correct amount.

The kanji for 'nine' is here accompanied by a single drop that changes the meaning entirely into that of 'Round'. Though this kanji refers to the shape of something, a number can too be considered 'round'. Here we turn 'nine' into a round number by adding a small 'drop'.
The only difference between the kanji for 'sun' and 'white' is the presence of the small 'drop' on top. To protect our skin from the 'sun', we often apply a 'drop' of white sunscreen.
'One' plus 'white', makes a hundred. One can imagine that the number 'one' sunscreen blocks 100% of the sun's rays.

It might be easier to think of this as a 'drop' + 'ten', though it can be broken down further to reveal the walking stick that is being driven through the horizontal floor through the power of a thousand drops.
You can break this down into its elements if you wish, but it might be easier to see this as simply a line passing through an opening marking its middle.

A pole accompanied by two small drops. Note how the drops are written after the central vertical stroke, and also that the central stroke contains a little hook at the end. The smallness here refers to the small drops, presumably small side effects caused by the larger central stroke.
Small plus an extra drop makes 'few'. Imagine a few drops of water hitting a window. After a while, the drops will slide down the window, creating a trail represnted by the final stroke.
Once again, you can break this down into its components if you wish, but this kanji symbolically represents a small line raised 'above' a larger line.
In contrast to the previous kanji, the small line now resides 'below' the large line. These two kanji become easier to remember when learned as a pair.
Have you ever been at a gathering or party that is lasting way too long into the evening? Well this magic wand allows you to teleport outside. The catch is that it only works in the evening.
Here a walking stick with a magic wand attached that automatically 'stops' things for the user.

We combine the elements for 'stop' and 'a few' that we just encountered to create the kanji for 'walk'. The etymological form of the stop element being a 'footprint' comes in handy here. We see 'a few footprints' to indicate where someone has been walking.
This kanji represents the 'correct' way to start a race, with the footprint just before the line. After all, putting your foot over the line before the race starts would not be correct.
Oneself here is represented by a single drop over an eye. If you've ever tried to put eye drops in, you'd know it can sometimes by tricky to administer them by oneself.
The kanji for mother here is a pictograph of two breasts. Take good care with the stroke order here; this is not the simple 'mouth' shape we are used to dealing with.
Every mother deserves a lie down. Or perhaps this kanji represents the collective experience of every mother having a child lie down on top of them.

The pictograph of a father here is considerably more abstract than that for mother. It might be easier to see the father's face here though, the two eyes represented by the first two strokes and then a nose that forms the outline of a moustache with the last two strokes.

A father with a pot lid on his head represents the idea of mingling or the meeting of people. Here we see a father who has put a pot lid on his head so that he can stand out in the crowd whilst mingling with other fathers.

A school is obviously a place where lots of pupils mingle, but what does this have to do with trees? Perhaps it is a really old building made from wood, or the tree represents the growth of the pupils whilst in attendance. However you imagine it, combine these two elements to create the kanji for school.

Be careful with the stroke order with this kanji. Here we see a strange conglomeration of strokes that look like elements. Can you see 'lie down', 'walking stick', perhaps the outline of 'correct' or 'stop'. This kanji is one of those rare occasions where simply learning the kanji as a unit is probably the simplest path forward.
The kanji for person is simply a pictograph of a person with two outsrtetched legs.
Here we see a pictograph of your chosen 'person' from the previous kanji resting against a 'tree'.

The kanji for 'body' differs from 'rest' by a single stroke. We saw this combination of 'tree' and 'one' earlier in the kanji for book. In a similar way to reading a book, you can tell a lot about a person by reading their body language.
This kanji has a striking resemblance to 'small', 小, except where the central stick in 'small' only produced two small drops, here we see two large splashes of water.
The kanji for ice is simply the kanji for water but with an extra drop. Now the form almost represents a snowflake.

'Water', 'drop', 'water', almost seems to tell the story of someone swimming. Notice how the vertical stroke appears to have a small handle at the top this time. We will encounter the right-hand side as a standalone kanji later.
The ultimate destination of each and every drop of water is ultimately the sea.
We see an old, possibly ancient, ritual of admiring the moon's reflection in the waters of a lake.
The idea of this kanji is something running alongside something else, or in accordance with. The kanji represnts this as water running alongside a gully.
Here an unfortunate execusion decision is to be made, either by water or by the guillotine.
Here we see a pictograph of a fire, or perhaps a person on fire! The two drops represent the smoke rising up from the flames.
